newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-In first test, US farm law means less wheat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-In first test, US farm law means less wheat.

text.p: In the first test of the new "Freedom to Farm" law, U.S. farmers slashed their winter wheat plantings to the lowest level in 19 years, the government said Friday.
Friday's report, which showed plantings of just 48.2 million acres, was the first indication of the effect of the new law, which lifted most federal controls on crop acreage.
"Farmers, with the opportunity to plant more, have planted seven percent less," private consultant John Schnittker said. Bad planting weather "is not the whole story by far," he said.
Other analysts said farmers turned their backs on lackluster wheat prices with an eye to switching to corn and soybeans.

"Freedom to Farm," reluctantly signed into law last April by President Clinton, was the biggest change in U.S. farm policy in 60 years. It removed most federal controls over agriculture, letting farmers grow virtually anything, in exchange for a cap on annual subsidy spending at half recent levels.
Grain-market analysts, who had expected plantings of 51 million acres, were startled by the Agriculture Department report.

"That's a tremendous drop, the three million acres," said Paul Haugens of FIMAT Futures in Chicago. Wheat prices leaped as much as 15-1/2 cents a bushel when trading opened at the Chicago Board of Trade but calmed somewhat later in the day.
"The precipitous drop in wheat prices (during 1996) caused farmers to shift away from wheat acres," said John Zanutto of LFG Futures, of Chicago.
A spokeswoman for Kansas Republican Senator Pat Roberts, the author of the law, said, "Farmers are planting what they see fit for their operations, and that was the intent of the legislation."
Farm policy analysts said the winter wheat figure should be regarded as a sign the new U.S. farm policy was working.

Robert Young, co-director of the Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute at the University of Missouri, said the largest declines in planting were in the Corn Belt. FAPRI had projected a decline in wheat acreage this year, but not as steep as indicated by the Agriculture Department report.
"Most folks expected in the Corn Belt, where wheat is not the dominant crop, ... that once you free those people up, they aren't going to want to plant wheat," Young said. "It's not that surprising."

Young said the next thing to watch would be reports on acreage in spring crops. It was likely most of the three million acres of wheat land would re-appear in corn or soybeans, "and probably more corn than soybeans," he said.

"This (wheat decline) implies there was some impact from Freedom to Farm," said Gary Blumenthal of analysts World Perspectives. He said some farmers were glad to be free of requirements to plant wheat in order to remain eligible for subsidies.
It was "definitely too early" to tell if "Freedom to Farm" would be a long-term success, Blumenthal said. Other analysts concurred.
"No, I don't think policymakers should start worrying yet," said Mike Hoover of WEFA Group in suburban Philadelphia. "They should stand back and see what happens this year" on crop size and prices.
"I'm expecting things to work. You probably will see some increased volatility from year to year."
